For count-changing category-level gaps, structured peer evidence matters more than ranker sophistication. The findings suggest that the rankings should guide analyst inspection rather than serve as automatic judgements of requirements completeness.
comment: Pre-review version of a paper subsequently accepted for publication at PROFES 2026

title: Architectural Design Decisions for Data Ingestion in Big Data Architectures
summary:
Introduction: Data ingestion is the first critical step in a data architecture, in which data from various sources is moved to storage systems, such as data lakes and data warehouses, for analysis and insight generation. When developing a data ingestion pipeline, practitioners (e.g., data engineers and architects) must understand the data ingestion requirements (functional and non-functional) and select appropriate design options to support them.
  Objective: To help practitioners systematically develop data ingestion processes, this paper aims to compile a catalog of data ingestion design decisions, their options, and the selection drivers.
  Method: We conducted a systematic gray literature review on data ingestion, analyzed the selected literature using qualitative data analysis methods, and conducted semi-structured interviews with experts to assess the framework's practicality and utility.
  Results: From 42 gray literature articles, we identified 8 architectural design decisions, 59 decision options, and 36 decision drivers to guide practitioners in the design and implementation of data ingestion pipelines. The framework was evaluated through expert interviews, assessing its completeness, simplicity, understandability, operational feasibility, and usefulness.

title: Plug-and-Play Sensor Evolution in Software-Defined Vehicles through Asset Administration Shells
comments: Peer-reviewed and Published in the 2026 IEEE 31st International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA)
summary:
Software-defined vehicles (SDVs) promise continuous software evolution, but sensor integration in deployed vehicles still depends on manual configuration, hardware-specific drivers, and repeated application-side adaptation. Existing standards address only parts of this problem. AUTOSAR standardizes selected sensor interfaces, the Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS) standardizes signal semantics, and Asset Administration Shells (AAS) standardize digital asset descriptions. However, these building blocks are rarely combined into an end-to-end onboarding path for sensors attached after vehicle deployment.
  This paper presents an AAS-driven plug-and-play sensor integration framework for safety-supervised sensors. Each sensor is represented by an AAS that combines hardware identification, interface metadata, VSS mappings, and references to containerized driver and optional application software. After physical connection, an edge gateway identifies the device, retrieves the matching AAS, deploys the referenced software, and publishes the resulting data under stable vehicle signal paths. A prototype on a resource-constrained edge gateway connected to an RR100 UGV demonstrates automated integration of a USB camera and an ultrasonic sensor. Across repeated integration cycles, the prototype reaches operational state in about 2s, shows no failed events, and keeps applications independent of hardware-specific interfaces. The results indicate that the introduction of AAS as an executable onboarding contract enables automated runtime deployment of sensor drivers in SDV environments.
comment: Peer-reviewed and Published in the 2026 IEEE 31st International Conference on Emerging Technologies and Factory Automation (ETFA)

title: When Code Works but the License Doesn't: Evaluating License Constraint Handling in Coding Agents
comments: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 VeriCode Workshop
summary:
Coding agents increasingly undertake repository-level development, including dependency selection, source modification, and software deployment. However, existing evaluations prioritize functional success over licensing correctness and commercial suitability.
  We investigate whether agents recognize and preserve software-license constraints when developing proprietary software. Experiments across multiple agents examine permissive and copyleft licenses, missing licensing information, transitive dependencies, source modification, dual licensing, vendoring, and distribution contexts. Agent traces, repository changes, and final artifacts are evaluated against licensing ground truth.
  Results reveal a persistent gap between functional and licensing correctness. Agents can successfully build and test software while overlooking licensing constraints involving provenance, authorization, and distribution. Better outcomes emerge when licensing information translates into engineering actions such as dependency substitution, architectural changes, and release gating. We argue that licensing in agentic development requires contextual constraint recognition and preservation across the software lifecycle, not merely license classification.
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 VeriCode Workshop

title: Optimal Development Path: An Empirical Evaluation of Tiered Dependency-Aware Sequencing
comments: 15 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Public aggregate benchmark results available on Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23762369
summary: The Optimal Development Path (ODP) in D-POAF orders Feature Blocks in a Wave Candidate by choosing the eligible block with the lowest effort-and-risk-to-value ratio (ERS/BVS), while respecting declared prerequisites. We evaluate native ODP (L0) against four dependency-aware strategies: unlock count (L1), unlocked value (L2), multi-hop potential (L3), and one-step rollout (L4), alongside local search, Sidney decomposition, and an exact reference. On held-out synthetic graphs with about one prerequisite per block, L0 attains 0.978 of the surrogate optimum at 12 blocks, versus 0.993 for L2 and 0.994 for L4. At 100 blocks, L0 attains 0.942 and L2 0.983. In contrast, 373 historical Jira sprints from 21 open-source projects in TAWOS, used as scheduling proxies rather than D-POAF Waves, contain sparse recorded dependencies. On these instances, L0 attains 0.998 of the surrogate optimum and is exactly optimal in 69% of sprints. Unlock bonuses calibrated on synthetic graphs do not deliver significant average gains on these sprint-derived instances and can worsen the surrogate. L4 never worsens the declared surrogate relative to L0, but this guarantee does not extend to operational outcomes. Retrospective calendar replays using recorded Jira durations show that surrogate improvements do not reliably improve value-weighted completion. The findings support keeping L0 as the default and presenting rollout and exact references as auditable alternatives. Dependency-valid sequences expose prerequisite readiness, but their effects on interruptions, rework, costs, and delivery times remain unmeasured.
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Public aggregate benchmark results available on Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23762369

title: LLMs for Software Vulnerability Prediction and Prioritization: A Review
summary: Large language models have moved beyond vulnerability detection into prediction, assessment, exploitability estimation, risk assessment and prioritization, yet the evidence for this shift has not been synthesised separately from the detection literature. In this systematic literature review, we examine how LLMs are used across those five task classes, how well they perform against established baselines, and what prevents their operational adoption. Following a prespecified protocol, we identified 197 records, removed 53 duplicates, and excluded 103 records at title and abstract stage. We assessed 41 full texts and finally retained 23 primary studies published between 2024 and 2026 after a six-question quality assessment. The review contributes a five-class taxonomy ordered by decision outcome, a method taxonomy covering prompting, tuning and retrieval or agentic architectures, an evaluation-practice audit, a bounded performance synthesis, and a deployment-barrier analysis. The main findings are that (i) assessment is the largest class (9 of 23 studies), ahead of risk assessment and prioritization (7 each); (ii) reported accuracy is highest where the label space is tightest and is not stable across evaluation periods; (iii) explanation usability is an audited evidence gap rather than a demonstrated capability; and (iv) reproducibility is the weakest reported dimension. We conclude that present systems should support analyst judgement rather than replace it, and we specify three validation studies that would settle the open questions.

title: Dependency Fabrication in Repository Deployment Agents
summary: Repository deployment agents set up the environment needed to run a software repository. They often treat passing tests as proof of a successful setup. This report examines how such agents behave when a working setup is impossible. Probe repositories were built with a dependency that the agents could not legitimately obtain. Passing tests therefore indicated fabrication, such as creating a stub to replace the missing package. Agents in Repo2Run and SetupX usually fabricated the dependency. Both harnesses mostly still marked these runs as successful. Rules against fabrication, whether given in the prompt or repository documentation, did not reliably prevent this behavior. On MinimalSetupAgent, which was built for this report, mitigations proposed in the reward-hacking literature were most effective when the agent received a direct rule and had a clear way to stop and report the problem. Under these conditions, neither Qwen3.5-Plus nor GPT-5.6 Luna cheated in any of the 16 runs. Applying the same mitigation to Repo2Run and SetupX also required a native tool call for escalation. In Repo2Run, it worked only after the prompt was also replaced with one that placed less emphasis on passing tests.

title: When Exact Inference Changes Code Selection: A Decision-Theoretic Analysis of B4
comments: 16 pages, 7 tables; full proofs and numerical checks
summary: When generated programs are ranked using generated tests, a more exact posterior computation need not improve the selected program. We characterize this distinction in the published B4 code--test model. Identical execution signatures reduce exact candidate marginalization to N summands and nonempty joint maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference to two weights per group. A prior--budget condition guarantees that B4's whole-group rule already attains MAP; a sharp finite correction bound certifies when candidate marginals must select the same group. All 2,421 default-setting comparisons on 807 development matrices select the same candidates. A prospectively specified validation on 1,345 execution snapshots from a separate public archive also finds no changes in 4,035 default-setting comparisons. Across 80 literature-derived priors, this new archive yields 85 changed top sets in 107,600 comparisons; only six coincide with failure of whole-group MAP. Under finite-test proxy labels, four changes increase and five decrease expected success. These descriptive changes span seven snapshots; per-prior mean differences range from -0.074 to +0.045 percentage points. The results do not recommend a tuned prior or a new performance method. Exact enumeration and independent high-precision checks support the formulas and decision diagnostics. A supplementary fixed-test analysis separates asymptotic failure from observational ambiguity. The contribution is a model-specific account of when an inference intervention can change a software-testing decision, and when its effect must be sought in the priors or evidence instead.
comment: 16 pages, 7 tables; full proofs and numerical checks

title: Checking Retry Transparency in Agent Tools
summary: A successful retry does not necessarily put the earlier attempt behind it. An old write may still overwrite a later acknowledged update; a partially executed file write may even empty a file after the retry has returned successfully. We study how to test the recovery guarantee behind an agent tool's local idempotence claim. Our prototype takes manually constructed, source-backed effect contracts and checks them at two levels: atomic retry-absorption obligations and bounded interleavings of successful-attempt microsteps. It emits model witnesses, conditional admission decisions, and explicit uncertainty when a completion boundary cannot be justified. The evaluation preserves a locally frozen purposive frame of 6 MCP components from 4 repositories; selected paths in 5 execute on the study machine and one backend remains unavailable. Real tests include file, graph, Git-index, document-update and browser bindings, together with a native Qdrant development matrix. In 27 missing-reply checks, the selective rule completes six justified workflows without an acknowledged goal violation, whereas strict coalescing completes none and blind retry completes nine with three violations. An intent-aware Porcupine specification independently agrees with all 156 complete-history oracles. These are mechanism-selected tests, not defect-prevalence estimates or a new linearizability algorithm. The contribution is an executable recovery-contract workflow that makes effect granularity, logical identity and completion assumptions testable rather than inheriting them from a tool annotation.

title: Repository-Grounded Rubrics for Execution-Free Evaluation of Coding Agents
comments: 31 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/faros-ai/repository-grounded-rubrics
summary: Coding agents are usually evaluated by running task-specific tests, but tests may be missing or incomplete, and running them requires a working environment for each repository. We adapt agentic rubrics, introduced for selecting among candidate patches, into an execution-free measure of how far a patch satisfies a task's requirements. An agent explores the repository before the change and writes weighted binary criteria, and a judge without tools scores a diff by the weighted share of criteria it satisfies. We validate the ordering this score produces against test outcomes on SWE-bench Verified, using 7,291 labeled patches from fifteen systems. Within the 400 tasks that have both resolved and unresolved patches, the mean per-task AUROC is 0.826 (0.838 on tasks not used to tune the rubric-generation prompt), and ranking systems by their failing patches closely agrees with ranking them by resolve rate (Spearman 0.968). Case analyses trace disagreements to tests that do not match the task, execution-blocking defects that the textual assessment misses, and errors in criteria or verdicts. The validation does not establish absolute score magnitudes or requirement satisfaction beyond agreement with tests, but rubric scores could complement tests where tests or execution environments cannot be assumed.
comment: 31 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/faros-ai/repository-grounded-rubrics

title: Edge Computing for IoT-Enabled Smart Cities: A Review of Middleware, Explainable AI, and User Behavior Analytics
summary: This review looks at cloud-IoT edge middleware for analyzing user behavior in smart cities, with a particular focus on linking behavioral analytics to energy-aware and mission-critical urban services. The topic sits at the crossroads of smart-city platforms, IoT sensing, edge/fog/cloud computing, service-oriented architectures, machine learning, explainable AI, privacy-aware governance, and energy-critical applications such as EV charging, energy demand, environmental exposure, crowd safety, and the operational resilience of urban infrastructure. As such, this paper maps out the main categories of user-behavior data, examines five application domains, compares several case studies, and puts forward a new XAI-EdgeSOA Middleware Framework called X-EdgeCity Middleware. This framework brings together IoT sensing, edge preprocessing, fog coordination, event-driven communication, cloud analytics, XAI explanations, privacy-by-design, and benchmark logging. The goal is to support not just general smart-city applications, but also energy-sensitive or mission-critical services, where latency, reliability, explainability, and accountability have a direct impact on urban safety and continuity of operations.

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Education for Software Developers: A Multivocal Literature Review
summary: Quantum computing threatens widely deployed public-key cryptography, making post-quantum cryptography (PQC) adoption a software engineering challenge. However, it remains unclear how well existing educational provision prepares software developers for secure PQC implementation and migration. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 8 research publications and 15 professional training offerings, examining competency coverage, practical software engineering tasks, pedagogical approaches, learner support, and evaluation. All 23 sources covered PQC foundations and algorithms, but coverage of practical software-engineering tasks was uneven. Our analysis identifies six gaps concerning developer focused evaluation, authentic software engineering tasks, task competency alignment, pedagogical design and learner support, security-focused assessment, and long term validation of learning outcomes and transfer. We derive recommendations for strengthening PQC education and better preparing software developers to implement and migrate cryptographic systems securely.

title: AppSec Core: An Ontology for Security-by-Design Software Engineering
comments: 24 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Supersedes OSF preprint doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/WG8PV
summary: When engineers or coding agents change an application, a dependency, a configuration or a build pipeline, they need to know three things: which security rules apply, how to meet them, and what evidence to leave. Today the answers are spread over many standards, frameworks, laws and lists of weaknesses, and each one uses its own words and level of detail. This paper presents AppSec Core, a model of the security work that engineers do. It says what must be true, which practices get there, which mechanisms do the job and which artefacts show that it was done. It has 259 elements in ten domains. We built it from a security-by-design manual written from practice, and then checked it against 31 outside sources, ten of them about AI systems and agents. Along the way we made three changes, which added five objectives and made one domain wider. We did not need a new domain. Most objectives are backed by several sources: the typical objective is used by six of the twenty technical sources, and 194 of the 202 objectives, practices and mechanisms are linked to items in the sources. For the domain of a change, the model gives back a closed set of typed elements, and for a source, it gives back the objectives that the source points to. We keep the model apart from the manual, the selection rules and the server that delivers the result, and we follow one change, adding a third-party package, through all four. When a code generator received the requirements, the share of security tests passed on a public benchmark went from 77.4% to 93.0%. On a second benchmark, the result was close to that of the benchmark's own "oracle" prompt, which is written with the tests in mind.
comment: 24 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Supersedes OSF preprint doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/WG8PV

title: Model Discovery for Virtual Chaos Engineering with Incomplete Tracing: An eBPF Study
comments: Submitted to Software and Systems Modeling journal
summary: Model-based fault experiments can assess the consequences of component failures before intervening in a running application. Recent work on model discovery and graph simulation acquired operation models from application telemetry and used them for availability prediction. Applying this approach to operational legacy systems raises an acquisition problem: the required traces may be absent or incomplete, while introducing them can require changes across heterogeneous components. These systems continue to serve business operations during extended maintenance and modernization. External observation offers a possible route to model-based fault analysis before a tracing retrofit, but collecting telemetry does not by itself establish that an executable operation model can be obtained. We investigate this route using extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) observations and the existing graph-based modelling approach. A 108-case study varied application software development kit (SDK) tracing across absent, partial and full conditions in three public applications. Discovered dependencies were combined with declared operation requirements, deployment facts and scenario assumptions; model forecasts preceded independent execution checks. With SDK tracing disabled, the tested OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation path supported all seven operations in two applications across three repetitions. Forecasts agreed exactly in 17 of 21 operation-repetition groups; the maximum state-weighted discrepancy was 4.22 percentage points. Combining observed context links supported nine additional groups under partial tracing. The results establish an acquisition path for virtual fault experiments under the tested observation constraints and identify limits imposed by protocols, evidence association and operation semantics.
comment: Submitted to Software and Systems Modeling journal

title: YUL: Bringing Software Supply Chain Security to Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents choose and declare third-party dependencies on their own. They often declare a stale version that they recall from their training data. A stale dependency exposes the project to known vulnerabilities that the latest release already fixes. We present YUL, a design for coding agent harnesses that ensures that no stale dependencies are ever used. It does so by checking every dependency declaration against the package registry. If a dependency is stale or does not exist, YUL blocks the usage and tells the coding agent which version to use, so the coding agent retries with the fix. We evaluate YUL on 60 tasks across six ecosystems with Claude Code running Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenCode running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Without YUL, Opus declares a stale version in 29% of runs and DeepSeek in 39%, and both declare a stale version in every GitHub Actions run. With YUL, the coding agents end on the latest release in 93% of stale Opus runs and in 96% of stale DeepSeek runs. YUL thus brings the best practices of software supply chain security to coding agents.

title: MRASLive: An online parameter estimation toolbox for time-dependent PDEs
summary: We present MRASLive, a toolbox for online parameter identification in time-dependent partial differential equations based on a model reference adaptive system (MRAS). Building on the MRAS proposed by Kaltenbacher and Nguyen (Inverse Problems 37(5) 2021) and its first numerical realization by the authors (Applied Mathematics for Modern Challenges 8 2026), the toolbox is designed for ease of use, utilising the user's weak form specification to prepare the data, the discretized MRAS and its solvers, and to verify the assumptions of MRAS's convergence theory semi-automatically.

title: Error Analysis of Deep Learning
comments: Mathematical survey of error analysis for neural network methods, with nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz method for elliptic PDEs as running examples. Covers function and Sobolev approximation, statistical estimation, and optimization error, together with stability estimates, convergence rates, and selected proofs
summary: This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.
comment: Mathematical survey of error analysis for neural network methods, with nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz method for elliptic PDEs as running examples. Covers function and Sobolev approximation, statistical estimation, and optimization error, together with stability estimates, convergence rates, and selected proofs

title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
summary: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

title: HydroMind: A Checkable Agent for Autonomous Hydrological Research
summary: General-purpose coding agents have written code for hydrological and Earth-system models. In these studies the researchers decided in advance how the model would be evaluated, for example the test period, the scoring function, and the standard the model had to meet. No study has tested what happens when the agent makes these decisions itself: how many of its claims are supported by its own data, code, and results, and whether readers can check them. Both may depend on the agent's harness, that is, the tools it can call and the written instructions it follows. We compared three harnesses: the agent's own harness; this harness plus the modeling tools of HydroMind, a hydrological modeling system we developed for general-purpose agents, which run every model through fixed commands and store its settings, trained model, and predictions; and both plus HydroMind's research procedure, under which the agent writes a research design before running any model and records every change to it. Under each harness, the same agent studied four open questions in hydrological model development and was given only the data. Under the three harnesses, the experiments submitted 23, 20, and 41 claims, each stating that one model or approach is better than, worse than, or similar to another. A claim does not hold if the difference recomputed from the experiment's own code and predictions disagrees with it, or if the code did not compare the two models or approaches the claim names. Under the three harnesses, 30%, 20%, and 5% of the claims did not hold. A statistical test, confidence interval, or decision rule that lets readers judge the stated difference was reported for 48%, 53%, and 83% of the claims. With the language model unchanged, changing only the harness reduced the share of claims that do not hold and increased the share that readers can check.

title: Sharp error estimates for Lagrange interpolation and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted $L_p$-spaces
summary: In this paper, we establish sharp direct and inverse approximation estimates for algebraic Lagrange interpolation polynomials and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted $L_p$ spaces on $[-1,1]$. A well-known limitation in the theory of approximation by interpolation polynomials states that for small rates of convergence $α\le 1/p$, classical moduli of smoothness fail to provide matching direct and inverse estimates due to the insufficiency of integral metrics to determine pointwise values at the interpolation nodes. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce new special semi-discrete measures of smoothness based on Steklov averaging operators, which combine global $L_p$-smoothness with discrete deviations from Steklov averages at the interpolation nodes. By using these measures, we establish fully matching direct and inverse approximation theorems for Lagrange interpolation polynomials, thereby providing complete two-sided characterizations of the rate of convergence for an arbitrary rate $α> 0$. As a natural application of the developed approach, we also obtain corresponding direct and inverse estimates, as well as strong converse inequalities, for Kantorovich-type operators constructed via Lagrange polynomials.

title: Numerical approximation of Benjamin-Ono type models for two-dimensional internal waves
summary: In this paper we analyze the numerical approximation with spectral methods of two asymptotic models for the two-dimensional propagation of internal waves in a two-layer system of fluids with rigid-lid condition. The semidiscretization in space of the periodic initial-value problem with the spectral Fourier-Galerkin method is introduced and some error estimates are derived. Then the semidiscrete system is integrated in time with the Implicit Midpoint Rule and several numerical experiments illustrate the performance of the corresponding full discretization.

title: Computing with Orientation-Dependent Vector Fields in Crystallographic Texture Analysis
summary:
We present a computational framework for representing orientation-dependent vector fields. Building on (arXiv:2608.21235), we translate the differential-geometric formulation into crystallographic notation and focus on its computational use in crystallographic texture analysis.
  In crystallographic applications, small orientation changes are commonly described by rotation vectors, spin tensors, or infinitesimal misorientations. By contrast, vector fields in harmonic computations are usually represented by components with respect to Euler-angle derivatives, following the classical formulation of generalized spherical harmonics. This representation is convenient but numerically unfavorable. We instead use rotation-vector components, extending a familiar description of individual orientation changes to orientation-dependent vector fields.
  In this representation, vector fields are described by three scalar component functions, which can be expanded into generalized spherical harmonics. We derive frequency-domain formulas for gradient, divergence, and curl, enabling their evaluation directly on harmonic coefficients. In particular, the gradient of a band-limited scalar function remains band-limited with the same bandwidth.

title: A level is not a rank: an empirical audit of quantile-to-index conversion in 10 released conformal-prediction libraries
comments: 34 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Online Resource (45 pages) included as an ancillary file. Code, probe outputs and pinned environments: doi:10.5281/zenodo.21799203
summary: Context. A conformal interval at 0.90 keeps that guarantee only at the right rank: a fresh score falls at or below the rth smallest of n with probability r/(n + 1). The libraries we study instead hand a level to a quantile function, which can land elsewhere. At n = 20, the upper end of statsforecast's interval sits at position 18.05 where rank 19 is required. Objective. Where does installed code resolve the wrong rank, at what cost in coverage, and what does it return when no rank reaches the level? Method. We audit 39 sites where a level becomes an index in 10 pinned packages, a named set rather than a systematic search. 12 are classified by running them, 11 through their shared numpy method, the rest from source. Coverage is paired against the required rank on the same scores. Results. All 7 tabular implementations reach the required rank. In darts, on one code path, coverage is unchanged (0.0000) where the ranks agree and 0.0280 to 0.0560 lower where they differ; a second archive repeats that split but not its range. Below the feasibility floor, $n < 1/α- 1$, of 14 public call paths 5 silently return a finite number; the rest raise or warn. Conclusions. Quantile interfaces take only a level; statsforecast's default calibrates below its floor. 6 of 19 upstream filings have merged, one fixing a coverage shortfall. A conformance suite classifies helpers by the rank they reach, and a checklist guides review.
comment: 34 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Online Resource (45 pages) included as an ancillary file. Code, probe outputs and pinned environments: doi:10.5281/zenodo.21799203

title: Training for sustainable scientific software in the AI era: from code production to scientific stewardship
comments: 10 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Submitted to Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
summary: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are changing how researchers interact with scientific software. Their effects on productivity vary across tasks and users, but they can weaken the connection between producing a successful computational artifact and retaining scientific command over the consequential choices and evidence on which it depends. For high-energy physics, this shifts part of the training challenge from code production toward scientific stewardship: researchers must be able to validate, explain, reproduce, maintain, and justify software and workflows partly generated or modified by AI. We argue that AI-aware software training should therefore combine dedicated instruction on AI systems with the integration of AI into established software and analysis training. Testing, provenance, reproducibility, resource judgment, and scientific validation should be exercised in AI-assisted workflows, with competence judged by the evidence supporting a result rather than by code generation alone. We frame this as a problem of sustainable scientific software: AI-assisted workflows should remain trustworthy and maintainable, use computational resources responsibly, and avoid making core competence unnecessarily dependent on privileged access to particular tools or infrastructure.
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Submitted to Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence

title: What Should an LLM Know? Knowledge-Guided Warm Starts for Software Optimization
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) process gigabytes in minutes; human experts work far more slowly. Prior studies that explored combinations of human/AI optimizers ignore this gap. Those studies asked systems or humans to label too many examples (e.g., SynthCore needs over four dozen per trial). Here, we test human and AI knowledge under a budget where evaluation is practical (a few dozen labels or fewer).
  We compare five baselines (random search, RRP, EZR, few-shot prompting, and a budget-matched SynthCore variant) against three ways to give an LLM domain knowledge before it proposes its first configurations: (1) AMP lists the domain's rules, then checks each candidate against them; (2) HKMA adds scouted data or documentation to the prompt; and (3) H-DKP has human experts correct the LLM's rules.
  We find that domain knowledge improves the "start-up" phase of LLM optimization, but only when that knowledge is checked, by the LLM itself or by a human expert. Across 49 datasets, unchecked knowledge did no better than few-shot prompting or EZR. On the other hand, AMP's self-checking variant (AMP-4) reached the best statistical rank in 44 of 49 datasets (budget-matched SynthCore: 23 of 49), and H-DKP did so in 7 of 8 expert studies. These checks cost little: half a cent of LLM calls per trial, or 6 to 10 expert contacts.
  Hence we say LLMs may not need more data, but rather their knowledge needs checking (and checking is cheap).

title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
comments: 36 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Software publicly available at https://github.com/RoryBarnes/vaibify
summary: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.
comment: 36 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Software publicly available at https://github.com/RoryBarnes/vaibify

title: Truthgate: Checking Coding Agents Against a Record They Cannot Edit - Cheating, Deterrence and Disclosure on Impossible Tasks
comments: 9 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Cygnux-Labs/Truthgate
summary: When a coding agent says it is done, is that true, and how would anyone know? We study this question in five steps; every paid study was pre-registered, and in each step the agent is checked against a record it cannot edit: tests re-run by the host and, from step 2 on, hidden checks in containers the agent never sees and a signed log of every tool call written by a signer outside the agent's sandbox. A pilot with a small local model (Qwen3.5-4B, 36 runs on impossible tasks) found no hidden failure, and showed that labels built from actions alone over-count lies. On Impossible-LiveCodeBench, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed 39 of 180 impossible tasks (21.7%), every time by special-casing its code to fit the failing assertion; Opus 5.5 (2.8%) and Haiku 5.5 (1.7%) rarely did. One sentence appended to the system prompt cut Sonnet's cheats on the same 60 tasks from 22 to 8 (an AI reviewer will read the transcript), 6 (a person will review the work), 6 ("This session is recorded.") and 1 (do not special-case tests), all significant under exact McNemar tests, with honest passes unchanged. No remaining cheat moved to a shell falsely described as unrecorded (0 of 4). Asked for a final report, every one of 55 natural cheats named its special case; unasked, Sonnet and Opus said nothing in 52 of 52. An LLM judge caught all 55; deterministic rules over the host record caught 27. A scripted tamper demonstration, with keyword stand-ins for the judges, shows that one rewrite of the agent-side transcript hides two calls from a judge that reads it, while the signed record keeps them; in a 40-rollout pilot, Sonnet never touched its transcript. The judge and the record caught different things, which leads to our main conclusion: the record is the evidence a judge should read, not a replacement for one. All pre-registrations, results documents, code and evidence manifests are released.
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Cygnux-Labs/Truthgate

title: RootSink: Reproducible C/C++ Crashes with Tested Repair Sites
summary: When a C or C++ program crashes on a crafted input, the line that crashes is often not the line that is wrong. Tools and models that repair or locate vulnerabilities need examples showing both, with evidence for each, which existing datasets rarely provide. RootSink provides 3341 records from 354 open-source projects. Most give the crash site a memory-error detector reported and a candidate location for its root cause, and label each with a weakness type and its evidence. For the 1954 records in the Reproduced tier, we re-ran the crash ourselves and confirmed that the fixed version runs cleanly. In 1275 of these, a single hunk of the developer's fix stopped the crash on its own. That marks a tested repair site, though not necessarily the defect, and 1273 records use it as the root. In a blind audit of an earlier version, two co-author raters called 68% and 92% of the tested repair sites they saw the defect, but only 37% and 51% of that version's located Reproduced-tier roots. RootSink ships with tasks, a patch scorer and run logs.

title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.

title: Management of Behavioral Addictions via Artificial Intelligence based Digital Technologies
summary: Behavioral addictions, such as problematic gaming, gambling, social media use, and online shopping, have emerged as a growing global concern with significant psychological, social, and economic consequences. Traditional assessment and treatment approaches, while clinically grounded, often struggle with scalability, accessibility, and long-term engagement. In recent years, advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the development of novel, data-driven solutions for the prevention, detection, treatment, and recovery of behavioral addictions. This book presents a comprehensive survey of the management of behavioral addictions through digital technologies, bridging clinical foundations with state-of-the-art computational approaches. This book aims to provide researchers, clinicians, and practitioners with a unified, interdisciplinary perspective on the opportunities and limitations of AI-based digital technologies in behavioral addiction management,and to highlight pathways toward more scalable, personalized, and effective intervention strategies.

title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
summary: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

title: BiMa-ECGSR: reconstructing the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with bidirectional state-space models
summary: Wearables and monitors record few electrocardiogram (ECG) leads; most diagnostic tools assume 12 leads. BiMa-ECGSR reconstructs the 12-lead ECG from reduced lead sets with a bidirectional Mamba state-space encoder--decoder, as regression (BiMa-SR) or diffusion (DiBiMa-SR). Models were trained on PTB-XL for six input sets (I; II; I+II; I+II+V1; I+II+V2; I+II+V1+V4), see only the measured leads at inference, and were tested on the PTB-XL test fold (2,198 records) and two external cohorts (Georgia, 10,275 records; Chapman-Shaoxing/Ningbo, 43,559). From lead II alone, the pooled median Pearson correlation (PCC) over the 11 predicted leads was 0.914 on PTB-XL, against 0.784 for a least-squares linear filter (lead I: 0.906 against 0.789). As limb leads are exactly derivable from I and II, multi-lead inputs were compared on predicted chest leads: 0.939 against 0.849 for I+II and 0.979 against 0.962 for I+II+V1+V4. BiMa-SR exceeded the linear comparator in all 18 configuration--cohort pairs (by 0.012--0.136), a margin that shrank as chest leads were added. From lead II, regression was more accurate than diffusion (DiBiMa-SR: 0.903 one-step, 0.862 with six DDIM steps). A 12-lead classifier trained only on real ECGs reached a superclass macro AUROC of 0.912 on real PTB-XL ECGs, 0.843 on reconstructions from lead II and 0.908 from I+II+V1+V4; externally, reconstructions from three or four leads scored within 0.004 of real ECGs. BiMa-SR (2.68\,M parameters) takes 45.8 ms per 10-s record on a GPU. Reconstruction makes reduced-lead recordings usable by 12-lead tools; it cannot add information absent from the measured leads.

title: Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents: State-Transfer Auditing and Controls in the Agent Harness
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.

title: SIGMA: speaker-isolated, symptom-structured multimodal estimation of depression severity from clinical interviews
summary: Clinical interviews are central to depression assessment but time-consuming and rater-dependent. Automated severity estimation offers scalable screening, yet existing methods often retain interviewer speech (confounding participant cues), fuse modalities late (losing fine-grained cross-modal dynamics), or score symptoms independently (ignoring inter-symptom correlations). We present SIGMA, a speaker-aware, symptom-structured framework for depression-severity estimation from semi-clinical interviews. SIGMA uses speaker diarization to restrict input to participant speech, cross-attention so that text, audio and video condition one another during encoding, and a graded-response head that predicts the eight questionnaire items jointly through a shared latent severity trait with item-specific ordered thresholds. On the Extended Distress Analysis Interview Corpus, SIGMA achieves state-of-the-art performance (CCC 0.762, RMSE 4.13, MAE 3.30 over five seeds). Ablations confirm that isolating participant speech and joint, structured symptom prediction each substantially improve concordance and estimation accuracy.

title: Systematic Mapping Protocol. Generative AI-Augmented Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study of Practices, Specifications, and Reuse in Software Development
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), is rapidly being adopted in requirements engineering (RE). Existing secondary studies have characterized which RE activities are supported and which prompting strategies are used, but little is known about the specifications that GenAI-augmented RE produces and how they are used in subsequent activities such as specification-driven development (SDD), design and code generation, test derivation, verification, and reuse. This document presents the protocol of a systematic mapping study (SMS) that will identify and classify research on GenAI-augmented RE, with particular attention to the work products it generates and their downstream use. The protocol defines the research questions and their classification schemes, the search strategy, the study selection procedure, the data extraction form, the analysis approach, the tool support, and the threats to validity. It is published in advance to establish a prior commitment and to support the transparency and repeatability of the study.

title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
summary: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.

title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
summary: When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

title: A Survey on RLOps for Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become increasingly important for improving the reasoning, instruction-following, and task-solving capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, scaling RL training exposes failures in distributed execution, feedback computation, and learning dynamics that can waste computational resources, slow training, and undermine model improvements. These challenges have motivated a growing body of techniques for LLM RLOps, which manages the efficiency and reliability of operations throughout the LLM reinforcement learning training lifecycle. Despite growing interest, these techniques remain scattered across research areas, with limited synthesis of their operational roles and interactions. To bridge this gap, we present a systematic survey of LLM RLOps methods. We organize existing approaches into five stages: Training Setup, Experience Collection, Reward Computation, Policy Optimization, and Model Evaluation. Within each stage, we examine operational concerns, management techniques, and evaluation evidence. Building on this taxonomy, we identify open challenges and future directions in training process observability, cross-stage coordination, generalizable RLOps, multi-run management, and RLOps for recursive self-improvement. These directions extend operational management from individual training runs to diverse training settings, shared infrastructure, and successive improvement cycles. We maintain a GitHub repository indexing relevant papers and open resources at https://github.com/zhanglingzhe0820/Awesome-RLOps.

title: Implementing Binary Transformers with Approximate Memories with Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) Protection
summary: Quantization is an effective technique to reduce memory storage, computation complexity and power for Transformers, and the binarization of the weights is important for meeting these requirements. Approximate memory can further reduce the power for memory, but it also introduces errors. Current research for binary Transformers focuses on task performance, but the model dependable operation against errors on the memory has not been well studied. In this paper, we first evaluate the dependability of binary Transformers with the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) as a case study. A large accuracy loss occurs only at high Bit Error Rates (e.g. BER = 5% or 10%). Then we propose a novel Permutation Invariance Enabled Selective (PIES) scheme to protect the binary weights at very low overhead. This scheme exploits the invariance of Transformers to permutations in the rows and columns to group the critical weights and perform selective protection on those weights. Simulation results show that PIES can recover most of the performance loss caused by bit errors at BERs as high as 10%, at an overhead significantly lower than traditional error correction schemes. These results confirm the feasibility of running binary Transformers using approximate memory with aggressive voltage scaling on resource-limited low power edge devices. The code for PIES is released on github (https://github.com/YangZhutian/binary-transformer-prefix-repair).

title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter
comments: 11 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Under review at the EACL 2027 Industry Track
summary: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Under review at the EACL 2027 Industry Track

title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
summary:
This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations.
  We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transformers. Issues uncovered by the survey include the lack of benchmark datasets for CA, which hinders the comparison of methods and the generalizability of ML models. The survey identifies the potential for explainable AI tools to help develop trust in decisions, and to drive forward CA research itself.

title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

title: Image Watermarking With Memory Across Reissuance
summary: Publishers often revise and reissue images, yet valid watermarks may persist on superseded releases or unapproved edits. Even a current release can contain regions last authorized at different revisions. We introduce and formalize reissuable provenance: determining an image's current, superseded, or unissued status and recovering each region's last authorized revision (its generation), with abstention when evidence is insufficient. Generational Stratigraphy Fields (GSF) combine watermark evidence with an authenticated live reference to the current release, enabling replacement or retirement without rewriting circulated copies. Each reissue freshly embeds new generation labels in approved regions and inherited labels elsewhere, preserving history without requiring old watermarks to survive successive edits. Our complete-output reissuance evaluation follows 480 histories through four releases, retaining each AI editor's entire output. GSF achieves 99.67% accuracy in classifying issued images as current or superseded and 94.09% recall of unissued edits. After three reissues, one generation map provides time and location: it recovers regional labels with 93.13% median accuracy and localizes the latest approved revision with 92.86% IoU. Regional labels remain readable under tested delivery transformations that impair issued-state recognition. Watermarks can thus express who issued an image, which release is authoritative now, and when each region was last authorized.

title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
summary: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
comments: 43 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables; includes supplementary information with 3 further figures
summary: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.
comment: 43 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables; includes supplementary information with 3 further figures

title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
summary: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
summary: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

title: Lossless Reversible Watermarking for AIGC with Applications in Authentication
summary: AIGC watermarking is commonly used for tracing, but it can also support applications such as authentication and tampering detection. We study lossless reversible watermarking, which enables exact recovery of the original watermarked image after permissible distortions. By exploiting the relatively low entropy of the information required for image generation, together with robust latent-space watermarking, we design a framework that preserves sufficient information for lossless recovery. We then apply the framework to AIGC authentication, which generally faces two key challenges. First, the authentication mechanism must resist adaptive adversaries. Second, the content relevant to authentication, such as visual designs or expressed messages, may depend on application requirements that are not known at generation time. To solve these difficulties, we incorporate cryptographic message authentication to provide unforgeability against adaptive attacks. Lossless recovery provides the original image as reference evidence, after which a suitable analyzer can be selected to make the authentication decision. Experiments on Stable Diffusion demonstrate exact recovery under a wide range of distortions.

title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
summary:
The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever.
  To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
summary: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

title: Incremental Roseland: Batch-wise Landmark Diffusion via Kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève Update
summary: Landmark diffusion (Roseland) computes a diffusion-map-style spectral embedding from the singular value decomposition of a degree-normalized data-to-landmark kernel matrix, at a cost far below that of full diffusion maps. It assumes, however, that all data are available at once. We introduce incremental Roseland (iRoseland), which casts the landmark affinity as a row-growing matrix whose SVD can be updated with a kernelized Sequential Karhunen--Loève (SKL) scheme. Degre correction is handled by a first order expansion about a reference mean kernel row and so that the landmark-side eigenbasis may be recovered from a single landmark-by-landmark eigendecomposition at each step. The presented method requires only a single pass over the data and runs in bounded-memory with state independent of the number of points processed.
