Project page: https://frankdengai.github.io/SciFigQual-Bench/

title: VETO: Towards Protecting Images From Frontier AI Editing
summary: Modern image editors blur the boundary between image editing and text-to-image synthesis, extracting people and objects from a single photo and inserting them into new scenes without subject-specific fine-tuning. Existing defenses struggle to disrupt such manipulations in these models without large, visibly damaging perturbations to the images. We introduce VETO, a white-box image-cloaking method for open-weight editors that maximizes the entropy of attention between reference image and generation tokens to disrupt selective retrieval of source details, while requiring neither the future editing instruction nor modifications to the model. We also introduce VetoBench, a benchmark of 300 benign and harmful tasks balanced between within-scene editing and recontextualization. Full Pareto evaluations on FLUX.2 and FIBO-Edit across three benchmarks and five perturbation budgets demonstrate overall better protection-fidelity trade-offs, particularly against recontextualization. Protected images remain effective on fine-tuned and distilled variants of the editor without reoptimization.

title: QAdapt: Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding for Surface-Code Quantum Error Correction
comments: 16 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables, including appendices. Revised and expanded version
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing relies on quantum error correction to protect logical information, requiring classical decoders that keep pace with syndrome generation. Heterogeneous, changing hardware noise and the distribution shift from simulation to experiment challenge the accuracy and robustness of fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt learns local spatiotemporal correlations, continually adapts across noise environments, and passes the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Online elastic weight consolidation limits forgetting as training moves between measurement, idle, CNOT, and Pauli-bias noise regimes. At distance nine, the HTNet pre-decoder reduces equivalent per-round logical error by 15.64% relative to Ising-Fast, with 28.75% fewer parameters and 9.07% less matching-backend time. Online EWC reduces average forgetting by 76.52% relative to sequential fine-tuning. With weights frozen, it reduces equivalent per-round logical error by 5.66% relative to continued base-environment training on a fixed valid domain of 331 unseen compound-noise conditions; whole-sequence failure probability falls by 2.54% over all 396 conditions. On native Willow records, the corresponding per-round reductions are 19.44%, 17.47%, and 17.95% at 10, 30, and 50 rounds, without target-domain fine-tuning. These results show how adaptive neural pre-decoding can improve logical accuracy, preserve performance across noise regimes, and reduce residual matching workload within an established decoding pipeline.
comment: 16 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables, including appendices. Revised and expanded version

title: Compact SAT and MaxSAT Encodings for Business-to-Business Meeting Scheduling with Idle-Time Balancing
comments: 6 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Revised version incorporating reviewer feedback; accepted for presentation at RIVF 2026
summary: Business-to-business meeting scheduling assigns pairwise meetings to slots and locations under availability, capacity, conflict, and precedence constraints. The published Boolean formulation retains removable assignments and uses pairwise precedence clauses. We combine solution-preserving domain filtering, sparse shared-suffix precedence encoding, and an objective minimizing the range of participants' internal idle-slot totals. Experiments on 126 official and 100 higher-density derived instances separate domain filtering, precedence representation, transitive relations, and optimization method. Under the same objective, the compact model achieves median paired reductions of 40.3% in clauses and 55.9% in peak memory relative to an adapted published MaxSAT formulation. Domain filtering alone reduces assignment variables by 24.1% and clauses by 16.2%. Suffix sharing gives an additional clause reduction of 0.5%-1.0% on official precedence instances, reaching 5.5% at the highest density in derived instances that retain a known feasible schedule. Total-time changes are small and mixed. Internal idle distinguishes short interruptions from longer waits; aggregate idle complements the range. In the original one-run comparison, all three SAT and MaxSAT methods solve every official instance with lower median total times than Gurobi.
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Revised version incorporating reviewer feedback; accepted for presentation at RIVF 2026

title: CADENA: Stepwise CAD Reverse Engineering
summary: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) underpins modern engineering, yet converting existing shapes into editable models still demands substantial expert effort. Most AI systems emit the entire CAD program in a single pass, never inspecting the intermediate geometry. In contrast, human engineers build a part feature by feature, checking after each operation what remains to be modeled. We introduce CADENA (Spanish for "chain"), a model that reconstructs a 3D mesh as a parametric CAD program, growing its sequence of operations one at a time and comparing the target with the currently predicted geometry at every step. We also address the lack of benchmarks for evaluating reverse-engineering methods on mechanical parts, introducing CADENA-Bench, a benchmark that measures performance across categories of mechanical parts. CADENA outperforms prior methods on CADENA-Bench and on the DeepCAD, Fusion 360, and MCB datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/zhemdi/cadena, model weights at https://huggingface.co/kulibinai/cadena, and CADENA-Bench at https://huggingface.co/datasets/kulibinai/cadena-bench.

title: Contour: Extensible Mapping Surfaces for Agentic Accelerator Kernel Generation
summary: Emerging accelerators rarely ship with mature compiler backends, so recent work asks LLM agents to write native kernels directly from ISA documentation and simulator feedback. On two such accelerators, this direct workflow returns a correct kernel on only 17 of 38 workload instances, and most of its inference budget is spent re-deriving machine semantics and repairing illegal code rather than optimizing the workload. We present Contour, which consists of two parts. Contour-Explore replaces native-code generation with search over a mapping surface: a typed set of scheduling knobs and their legal domains, generated automatically from the accelerator's ISA description and the workload graph. A compiler-owned resolver completes partial assignments into legal plans and emits native code, so every evaluated candidate is verified against the compiler's default, and any policy can drive the search, including hill climbing, evolutionary search, and LLM agents. Compared with KernelCraft, a state-of-the-art agentic kernel generator, an LLM agent through Contour-Explore returns a verified kernel on every Gemmini and PLENA instance, produces 2.86x and 1.13x faster kernels on the instances where both succeed, and uses 26.3% and 83.4% fewer tokens per verified kernel. Contour-Ext extends the surface when search stalls: an LLM agent implements a new knob and its lowering in the compiler backend, and Contour-Ext accepts the extension only if the default path is byte-identical, every new value is numerically correct and changes the program, and the enlarged surface yields a measured gain. On VTA, Contour-Ext extends the AutoTVM surface of TVM, and AutoTVM's XGBTuner then finds 4.14x faster kernels; on PLENA, the extended surface makes the kernels found by hill climbing 1.20x faster.

title: CoNav-UAV: Cooperative Dual-Altitude Aerial Navigation via Stackelberg Learning
comments: 27 pages, 10 figures. Revised manuscript with expanded analysis and experiments. Removed an AAAI copyright notice inadvertently included through the template in the previous version
summary: Aerial search missions often require an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to locate a target from only a brief description of its appearance and surroundings, a task known as target-oriented aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN). The task demands city-scale exploration and grounding as well as collision-free close-range approach, two interleaved processes that are difficult to reconcile within a single agent. Most existing methods adapt the ground VLN paradigm to a single UAV and rely on external assistance to compensate for its inefficiency. A recent attempt deploys two UAVs at complementary altitudes but still depends on privileged sensing and trains the two agents independently, precluding any mutual adaptation. We propose CoNav-UAV, which models the task as a Stackelberg game between a high-altitude leader and a low-altitude follower to capture their sequential decisions and asymmetric observations and utilities, with both agents using only onboard sensing. We introduce Iterative Stackelberg Learning, which tailors optimization to each agent's role: the leader's high-level vision-language reasoning builds on pretrained capabilities and is refined through memory-based in-context learning, while the follower's precise motion control is fine-tuned through DAgger-style expert distillation. Alternating the two updates lets each agent continually adapt to the other's evolving behavior. CoNav-UAV outperforms single- and dual-agent baselines across three high-fidelity urban scenes from the AerialVLN benchmark. It improves success rate by up to 30.8 points on the learning scene and by up to 9.0 points under cross-scene transfer, where the leader reuses its learned memory and the follower is adapted with 2.6-3.7 times less target-scene data. Extensive ablations confirm the contributions of key components and the benefit of mutual adaptation, with consistent gains across VLM backbones.
comment: 27 pages, 10 figures. Revised manuscript with expanded analysis and experiments. Removed an AAAI copyright notice inadvertently included through the template in the previous version

title: MANGO-Grasp: Mahalanobis Fields over Geometry-Oriented 3D Gaussians for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping
summary: Cross-embodiment dexterous grasping aims to synthesize stable grasps across heterogeneous multi-fingered hands with little or no embodiment-specific tuning. Existing interaction-centric methods achieve promising results, but their object representations often underrepresent local surface geometry, hand descriptors do not explicitly capture both morphology and kinematics, and hand-object interaction modeling is typically isotropic. We propose MANGO-Grasp, an anisotropic interaction framework that represents objects as geometry-oriented 3D Gaussian primitives to better preserve local surface geometry, and encodes hands into pretrained descriptors that capture both morphology and kinematics. Hand-object interaction is modeled using anisotropic Mahalanobis fields that reflect the directional nature of contact and guide a shared optimization for grasp realization across embodiments. On the CMAP and MultiGripperGrasp benchmarks, MANGO-Grasp outperforms the strongest seen-hand baseline by up to 8.24 percentage points in simulation. It also transfers zero-shot to the unseen SharpaWave hand, improving over the strongest zero-shot baseline by up to 16.57 percentage points, and achieves 86% success in real-world experiments. The code and additional materials are available at https://connor-zh.github.io/MANGO-Grasp/.

title: Localize, Don't Beautify: Client-Side Control of Image-Editing APIs for Cosmetic Surgery Previews
comments: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Pilot study; no surgeon ratings. Code and paper source: https://github.com/suxrobGM/localize-dont-beautify
summary: Ask a commercial image editor to preview a cosmetic procedure and it will often change more of the face than the request names: a jawline edit can also smooth the forehead or alter the eyes. Existing methods for confining an edit to one region require access to the model's internals, which a public editing API does not expose. We ask how much control is possible from the client side alone. In a pilot benchmark, five current commercial editing configurations perform facelift-style jaw-neck and rhinoplasty edits on synthetic faces under two levels of client-side control: the prompt alone, and a masked composite that cuts the edited region out of the response and pastes it back onto the original photograph through a landmark-derived mask. Of 162 attempted edits, 151 could be scored. ArcFace cosine measures identity preservation; a CIELAB pixel-change ratio measures how much change lands inside the requested region rather than a protected facial zone. On 15 faces, the masked composite improved localization over the paired prompt-only output by a median of 0.315 (95% face-clustered bootstrap interval 0.279-0.366) while retaining most of the target-region change. Editors differed in edit strength and identity retention, and one returned near-copies for the facelift request. This is a study of control, not clinical accuracy: the faces are synthetic, no surgeons rated the outputs, and each condition was generated once. Within that scope, keeping a surgical preview inside its intended region needs no access to the model; a mask and composite on the client enforce it across every editor tested, at low provider cost.
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Pilot study; no surgeon ratings. Code and paper source: https://github.com/suxrobGM/localize-dont-beautify

title: Graph-of-Thoughts for LLM Causal Discovery with a Fairness-Pathway Case Study
summary: Methods that use large language models (LLMs) for causal discovery reason locally, deciding one variable pair or one node at a time, so they never compare alternative whole graphs. We introduce GoT-CD, a Graph-of-Thoughts method that asks an LLM for several complete candidate graphs from variable metadata alone, ranks them with a deterministic validity score, merges them under a hard union constraint, refines the merge, and projects the result to a DAG. We evaluate on Asia, Child, and an Alzheimer's disease graph with 100 samples and GPT-4o-mini. Over five seeds on Alzheimer's and Child, GoT-CD gives the highest mean F1 score and the lowest mean structural Hamming distance of the LLM methods, with 95% intervals of the difference excluding zero in seven of eight comparisons, and it returns a DAG in every run while using three LLM requests per graph. Replaying the logged runs without individual components attributes most of the gain to generating and merging several complete candidates. A case study on the effect of Sex on MOCA Score in the Alzheimer's graph shows the limits of structural scores: the fairness verdict drawn from the discovered graph disagrees with the reference verdict in twelve of fifteen LLM runs, including all five GoT-CD runs, which mostly drop the edge out of Sex. Graphs meant for a specific downstream analysis should therefore also be checked on the pathways that analysis depends on.

title: JUDOR: CTDE-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for the Co-Optimization of Joint UAV Motion and Decentralized Opportunistic Routing in Delay-Tolerant Network
summary: The growing deployment of delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) has made store-carry-forward (SCF) communication indispensable for operating under sparse intermittent connectivity. However, intermittent contact opportunities, finite node buffers, and limited message time-to-live (TTL) degrade message delivery performance and induce network congestion. Yet unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with extended radio coverage and controllable trajectories, can bridge ground-node pairs that would otherwise suffer poor connectivity. Nevertheless, conventional routing schemes decouple UAV motion control from message replication, and consequently fail to leverage UAV mobility to proactively create future contact opportunities. This paper presents JUDOR (Joint-UAV-Decentralized-Opportunistic-Routing), a centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework optimized for joint discrete UAV heading control and decentralized opportunistic routing. Specifically, we model the tightly coupled UAV motion-routing co-optimization task as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with a shared team reward. JUDOR adopts decentralized actors for local-node execution and a centralized critic used exclusively in training, with optional multi-horizon congestion-hotspot auxiliary supervision. Through evaluation across four distinct traffic modes, JUDOR yields consistent performance gains over both classical and learning-based DTN baselines, including PRoPHET and MaxProp, whilst preserving contact-limited decentralized execution suitable for real-world DTN deployments.

title: Scrouting: Cost-Aware Routing of Coding Agents by Scouting the Repository First
summary: Frontier language models can resolve repository-level software issues, but each attempt is expensive, and existing routers select a model from the issue text alone. We present SuperScout, which routes after scouting the repository: a 7B searcher, SuperScout-7B, first explores the repository and produces a structured handoff whose reproduction claims are sandbox-verified, with false claims stripped before delivery. The searcher's hidden states, together with the task text, then feed a resume-based router that dispatches the task to one of four frontier fixers. Adding a new fixer requires no retraining. On the full Python slice of SWE-bench Pro (266 tasks) under the benchmark's official capped budget tier, SuperScout matches the best single model's solve rate (159 of 266 for SuperScout, 158 for the best model) at about a fifth of the total cost per solve, and the reported configuration sits above the random traffic-splitting baseline. A no-router ablation, always the cheapest fixer with the handoff, ties the routed system on this benchmark, so the handoff rather than the routing decision carries the result. A paired calibration study points to the mechanism: the handoff appears to redistribute rather than add solving ability, lifting the three cheaper fixers while slightly hurting the strongest, though at $N=99$ the per-fixer effects are directional only; the searcher's hidden states improve cost routing on the calibration labels while the handoff's own text does not. The searcher's compute adds less than half a cent of GPU time per task.

title: OmniEdit-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Instruction-based Video Editing
summary: Instruction-based video editing (IVE) offers diverse applications, yet evaluating editing models remains challenging. Existing benchmarks suffer from two key limitations: narrow task coverage inherited from image editing that overlooks video-specific dimensions, and metrics that inadequately capture instruction fidelity, allowing visually plausible but incorrect edits to receive high scores. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniEdit-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark covering spatial, temporal, audio, and reference-based editing. It distinguishes between explicit and implicit instructions and incorporates reasoning-based scenarios to reflect real-world editing requirements. We further propose an evaluation framework that assesses accuracy, preservation, realism, and consistency using both human judges and a state-of-the-art vision-language model (VLM). An accuracy-aware penalty mechanism conditions the other three scores on accuracy, prioritizing instruction fidelity and penalizing plausible but incorrect edits. Experiments on prominent open-source and commercial IVE models reveal substantial room for improvement. OmniEdit-Bench provides a structured testbed for identifying model limitations and advancing instruction-based video editing. Project page: https://omniedit-bench.github.io.

title: The Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark: Evaluating Frontier LLM Tendencies in Escalation, Proliferation, Non-Proliferation, and Arms Control Scenarios
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are entering defense and national-security workflows. Seven of the nine nuclear-armed states have committed to keeping humans in control of decisions to use nuclear weapons, but LLMs may still shape the assessments and options that reach decision-makers. Scrutinizing that influence calls for evidence about how these models behave on nuclear-policy questions. Such evidence should cover more than crisis escalation and should separate a model's tendencies from artifacts of a single phrasing, ordering, or run; evaluations to date have not focused on these questions. We introduce the Nuclear Decision-Making Benchmark (NDM Bench), a dataset and reproducible framework for testing how the choice of model and the design of a question shape LLMs' answers on nuclear policy. Its 151 scenarios, written by international relations experts, span four domains: nuclear escalation (76), arms control (25), non-proliferation (25), and proliferation (25). Each scenario can be posed with different states in the decision-maker's role and with added framing sentences. Eight frontier LLMs answered every prompt five times, about 380,000 responses in all. Results highlight that models' choices differ by model and domain, and that in escalation, how often they choose a nuclear threat or nuclear use depends on the state being advised and, for some models, the framing. However, agreement across identical runs is often low, with all five runs agreeing on only 43% of escalation prompts. We release the scenarios, the prompts with their answer orders, and the parsed responses, along with documentation of how they were built and recommended practices for evaluations where there is no correct answer to grade against.

title: Beyond Routing Weights: Faithful Response-Level Interpretation of Mixture-of-Experts Reward Models via Contribution Contrast
summary: Reward models are central to learning from human preferences, yet identifying what drives their predictions remains challenging. Recent sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reward models seek to improve interpretability by routing prompts to specialized experts and characterizing experts through examples with high routing weights. However, routing weights only reveal which prompts an expert $\textit{receives}$, not how it $\textit{judges}$ responses, providing only a partial account of expert behavior. We therefore propose $\textbf{Co}$ntribution-$\textbf{Co}$ntrast ($\textbf{CoCo}$) response-level interpretation, which faithfully characterizes experts' roles using chosen-rejected response pairs with the largest contribution contrasts, jointly capturing routing and preference behavior. Across automatic and human evaluations, CoCo yields more coherent, faithful, and specialized interpretations than router-based, score-based, and sparse autoencoder-based alternatives while maintaining competitive reward modeling accuracy. Overall, we provide a controlled study of how different example-selection signals affect the interpretability of MoE reward models.

title: CS-PIKAN: Curvilinear Separable Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with Autograd-Based Metric Evaluation and Certified Error Bounds for PDEs on Complex Domains
summary: Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (PIKANs) offer effective neural solvers for partial differential equations (PDEs), but their conventional formulations rely on Cartesian domains and scattered collocation points, often resulting in high computational costs, approximate boundary enforcement, and no rigorous error guarantees. We introduce CT-PIKAN, which maps curvilinear domains to the unit square and computes all geometric quantities, including those required by the Laplace-Beltrami operator, through automatic differentiation. Building on this transformation, Curvilinear Separable PIKAN (CS-PIKAN) represents solutions as rank-R sums of products of one-dimensional KANs with topology-adapted bases (Fourier for periodic and Chebyshev for bounded coordinates and time). A separable envelope and transfinite lift enforce boundary and initial conditions exactly, while a single sqrt{g}-weighted residual is minimized on a stratified tensor grid, reducing network cost from the product to the sum of grid sizes. We derive a metric-explicit Poincar'e constant, establish computable a-posteriori error bounds for elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic problems, and prove that the loss provides an unbiased estimator of the squared residual norm underlying these bounds. Nine benchmarks cover advection, Poisson, and heat conduction on Cartesian, polar, wavy, annular, star-shaped, and sampled-boundary domains. Across three seeds, CS-PIKAN reduces the relative L2 error of CT-PIKAN by factors of 7-126 at equal or lower training cost (up to 10 times faster), with all certified bounds satisfied. Ablations highlight the importance of exact periodicity and boundary constraints; KAN factors outperform MLPs for transport-dominated problems but not smooth elliptic ones. Nevertheless, classical body-fitted solvers remain substantially cheaper at comparable accuracy for these two-dimensional linear problems.

title: What Should Visual Place Recognition Be Invariant To? Rethinking Condition Invariance in Visual Place Recognition
comments: 13 pages, 16 figures, 7 tables, including 4 pages of supplementary material
summary: Condition invariance in Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is typically evaluated by matching queries from one condition against a database from another condition. This tests the ability to recognize the same place when the query's condition differs from the database's condition. However, to map large environments, a database can be built from images collected by multiple robots or across multiple traversals under different conditions. In this setting, condition blindness---the ability to remain invariant to condition differences among database images---becomes important, but standard cross-condition evaluation does not provide a controlled assessment of this ability. Therefore, we introduce Distractor-Augmented Recall (DAR) to measure condition blindness in a controlled manner. Across eleven methods and six datasets, we find that differences in condition blindness can be larger than Recall@1 alone would suggest. To improve the condition blindness that DAR reveals, we compare three methods that make VPR descriptors more invariant to condition changes through post-processing. Among the three methods, we demonstrate INLP on a database built from multiple traversals under different conditions, showing that it can improve the performance of existing VPR methods.
comment: 13 pages, 16 figures, 7 tables, including 4 pages of supplementary material

title: Projection-Retraction MPPI: Exact Command-Space Constraint-Manifold Control for Manipulators
comments: Accepted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). 8 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/prmppi/
summary: Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is widely used in manipulation for its gradient-free, parallel handling of non-convex costs. Manipulation tasks, however, often impose constraints that hold throughout the motion: a closed kinematic chain that two grasping arms keep exactly, or joint limits and obstacle clearances that are never crossed. Standard MPPI handles such constraints only through the cost, as soft penalties that hold approximately and fail under a strong task cost. To address this, we propose Projection-Retraction MPPI (PR-MPPI), which enforces the constraints inside the sampled dynamics. At every rollout step, the sampled velocity is projected to satisfy both constraint types: the equality restricts it to a subspace, and each inequality to a half-space within that subspace, so inequality handling never breaks the equality. This projection, however, satisfies the constraints only to first order, and a finite step leaves a small drift off the equality. Therefore, we retract the returned command back onto the constraint, so that the commanded configuration satisfies the equality to numerical tolerance, independently of task weighting. We validate PR-MPPI on 14-DoF dual-arm systems. In simulation, the returned commands satisfy the closed-chain equality to numerical tolerance through a joint-limit stress test and randomized obstacle avoidance, while the measured trajectories retain the joint-limit and obstacle margins. On real hardware, the arms of a Unitree H1-2 humanoid reactively avoid a moving obstacle. Code and experiment videos are available at https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/prmppi/.
comment: Accepted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). 8 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/prmppi/

title: CommitKV: Commit-Aligned KV Cache Compression for Multimodal Agents
summary: Multimodal agents gather visual evidence through reasoning and tool use, extending their ability to solve tasks beyond the initial input. However, accumulating observations increases KV cache memory and inference costs. Token eviction reduces these costs by retaining useful cached tokens. Existing methods use attention, redundancy, or stage-specific queries to rank tokens, without explicitly comparing the same history across tool interactions. When observations shift attention, they may mistake temporarily reduced influence for lost usefulness and evict information needed later. We propose CommitKV, a training-free KV cache compression method that accounts for this changing evidence use. Commit-aligned measurement compares the deletion effects of the same page before a tool call completes and after its observation returns. Lifecycle-aware compression retires pages with low influence in both windows and temporarily protects pages influential before the call. Joint scoring combines attention importance, key redundancy, and token-level deletion effects to fill the remaining budget. Extensive experiments cover four open-weight multimodal models and eight benchmarks. CommitKV achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared compression methods on all four models. On Qwen3-VL-8B, it achieves 69.85% at a 512-token budget, only 0.91% below FullKV, and exceeds the strongest compression baseline by 8.44% at 256 tokens. Deploying the Qwen3-VL-8B agent with SGLang and vLLM at a 256-token budget reduces peak allocated GPU memory by 54.37%-55.23% and accelerates end-to-end inference by 2.12-2.17$\times$ over FullKV on the matched workload.

title: Biomedical Knowledge Composition: A Software Engineering Perspective
summary: Biomedical research has accumulated vast molecular, clinical, and population data, yet translating this wealth into actionable knowledge remains constrained by technical and organizational difficulties. This article presents a unified treatment of two perspectives on biomedical knowledge infrastructure. The first introduces the biomedical domain to software engineers: it explains why knowledge graphs (KGs) are the central integrative data structure in modern biomedicine, characterizes five data harmonization challenges (identifier mapping, entity resolution, schema alignment, evidence integration, and provenance tracking), surveys application domains from drug discovery to digital twins, and profiles six representative KG systems with contrasting choices. The second perspective asks why engineering biomedical knowledge infrastructure remains so difficult. We argue that a contributing root cause is limited adoption of software tooling and practices that make development in other mature domains - particularly web engineering - reliably composable and reproducible: package management, typed namespaces, canonical interchange formats, service composition protocols, reproducible pipelines, and lifecycle governance. Against this backdrop, eight open engineering challenges for biomedical data integration are catalogued, each with partial solutions but no universally adopted stack. Crucially, the article shifts emphasis from describing deployed KG instances toward the reproducible process of assembling them: reusable build pipelines, versioned dependencies, and engineering practices that let others compile and customize a KG from source rather than consuming a static artifact. Together, the two perspectives provide domain grounding for newcomers and a research agenda for software engineers seeking to make transformative contributions to biomedical knowledge infrastructure.

title: Linearized 2-Simplicial Attention
summary: We present a linearized form of 2-simplicial attention by rewriting the trilinear score as an inner product between a composite query and a key, so that the sum over keys takes the same form as ordinary softmax attention. We then approximate this sum with positive random features and store all previous keys in a fixed-size state, while the sum over second keys stays exact over all previous tokens. This reduces the cost from cubic to quadratic in sequence length, and both keys range over all previous tokens, which windowed 2-simplicial attention does not allow. We implement it with custom Triton kernels and combine it with Kimi Delta Attention to build a model with no softmax attention at all. With 15B equal training tokens on FineWeb-Edu, this model lowers validation loss from 2.35 to 2.32 over a KDA hybrid and lowers LAMBADA perplexity from 40 to 38.

title: Techno-Economic Boundary Analysis of Small Modular Reactor Cogeneration for Hyperscale Data Center IT and Cooling Loads
summary: Growing data-center electricity demand has increased interest in colocation with small modular reactors, but the conditions under which reactor power and steam-driven cooling reduce energy costs remain uncertain. Cooling can account for 20-40% of facility electricity use, making steam extraction a potential source of savings as well as a loss of turbine generation. We co-optimize hourly reactor dispatch, steam extraction, absorption cooling and grid exchange for a 200 MW$_\mathrm{e}$ data center in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) region, using a 109-entry scenario set spanning capital, market, policy, financing and cooling efficiency. At 2023 mid-range reactor capital, the nuclear configurations cost 54.9-67.7% more than grid supply even with the Section 45Y production tax credit. With the other 2023 assumptions held fixed, cogeneration reaches grid parity near \$5000 kW$_\mathrm{e}^{-1}$. At nth-of-a-kind capital, nuclear supply is 85.9-98.7% cheaper than grid procurement in 2023, but between parity and 34.8% more expensive in the low-price 2024 market. A carbon price of \$53.1-64.0 tCO$_2^{-1}$ closes the mid-range gap when exports receive credits at the hourly average grid emission factor; the resulting negative balances are attributional and do not represent physical carbon removal. Absorption cooling responds to hourly electricity prices and supplies 32.6% of annual cooling, but adds \$9.7 million yr$^{-1}$ relative to the reactor-only plant. Absorption breaks even at an installed cost of \$26 kW$_\mathrm{c}^{-1}$ at baseline efficiency and \$529 kW$_\mathrm{c}^{-1}$ on a legacy-efficiency campus, compared with surveyed commercial prices of \$450-1200 kW$_\mathrm{c}^{-1}$.

title: TEA: Text Encoder Alignment for Robust Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models can be misused to generate harmful content through adversarial or paraphrased prompts that bypass built-in safety mechanisms. Existing concept erasure methods often suffer from limited robustness against adversarial prompts, degradation of benign generation quality, or reliance on inference-time interventions that introduce persistent computational overhead. To address these limitations, we formulate concept erasure as a domain alignment problem in the text representation space. We propose a lightweight Text Encoder Alignment framework (TEA) that fine-tunes only the text encoder while keeping the generative backbone fully frozen. Given concept-anchor prompt pairs, our method trains a discriminator to distinguish token-level representations of concept-bearing prompts from those of safe anchor prompts, while updating the text encoder to make these representations indistinguishable. TEA introduces zero inference-time overhead and trains in seconds with only a few fine-tuning steps, making it practical for large-scale deployment. Despite this efficiency, TEA achieves state-of-the-art erasure robustness against black-box and white-box adversarial attacks on Stable Diffusion v1.4, while preserving generation quality on benign prompts. Furthermore, TEA is model-agnostic and achieves the lowest attack success rate on Stable Diffusion v3.5, extending concept erasure to Rectified Flow Transformer architectures with T5 conditioning, which remain largely unexplored by prior methods. Code is available at https://github.com/alirezafarashah/TEA

title: A Layered Simplex Architecture for Large Alphabets
summary:
A learning architecture induces a prior over its expressible models. Recent work links architectural success to a broad complexity spectrum: model probabilities spanning many orders of magnitude. Understanding how depth shapes these priors and prediction may help explain the success of neural networks and transformers.
  We study this connection in large-alphabet prediction through the *layered simplex architecture* (LSA), which multiplies independent uniform simplex vectors coordinate-wise and normalizes. At depth zero, the prior is concentrated on the uniform distribution; at depth one, the Bayesian predictor is Laplace's rule. Each additional layer shifts prior mass toward more concentrated distributions.
  We derive exact Bayesian marginal likelihood and regret expressions using reusable depth-specific kernels. Mixing over depths up to a cutoff logarithmic in alphabet size yields an explicit predictor with rigorous guarantees. For targets uniform on a specified sparse support, the mixture's prior complexity is asymptotic to the support-description cost at every fixed positive KL resolution, establishing a broad complexity spectrum.
  We also prove a regret lower bound for every label-invariant predictor: the expected description length of the discovered symbol set minus the source's uncertainty about its identity given its size. For Zipf sources in a growing-alphabet regime, the depth mixture attains this bound to leading order. Thus, the symbol-discovery rate determines the regret exponent. Although introduced to study depth, the LSA predictor competes with established large-alphabet methods, including Good--Turing, Ristad's law and an adaptive Dirichlet mixture, while substantially outperforming classical add-constant rules on concentrated sources.

title: The Cost of Synchronization in GPU Scale-Up Domains
summary: GPU scale-up domains are the building blocks of machine learning infrastructure. Architects provision the size and bandwidth in these domains assuming all GPUs reach a collective operation at the same time. However, we find that this assumption does not hold in practice. Across 300,000 collectives from training four language models on A100, H100, and H200 domains, GPUs reach the same collective hundreds to thousands of microseconds apart, despite running identical kernels. Since a collective cannot complete until every GPU contributes its data, GPUs that arrive early wait for the slowest one. We call this waiting time the synchronization tax, and it consumes nearly 40% of tensor-parallel communication time in an 8-GPU domain. To find its source, we develop an algorithm that recovers the chain of operations that delays each GPU before a collective. Our algorithm attributes 78% of the tax to variation in the runtimes of matrix-multiplication (GEMM) kernels across GPUs. Since the tax depends on the slowest of many GPUs, our analytical model shows that it grows at least logarithmically with domain size. Thus, a 72-GPU domain requires 3.3x more per-GPU bandwidth than today's simulators predict to keep communication below 12% of step time, and the optimal scale-up fabric should partition a switch's capacity among fewer GPUs with more bandwidth each.

title: Graph-Native Attention Acceleration for Attack Detection in Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: Cyber-physical systems (CPSs) rely on extensive networks of sensors, controllers, and actuators, making them highly vulnerable to attacks targeting measurements, control logic, and equipment operations. While graph-based attack detectors, especially graph attention models, efficiently localize such attacks by exploiting the communication and physical interaction graphs. The computational cost of edge-wise attention scales poorly with the number of interactions. This bottleneck severely limits the scalability of online monitoring in large or densely connected CPSs. To address this challenge, we introduce GraphGHHA, a graph-native attention acceleration layer designed to reduce the inference cost of graph attention mechanisms in CPS security. GraphGHHA consists of a local attention unit (LAU) and a global attention unit (GAU). The LAU captures the local interactions by restricting the attention computation of each node of a CPS to a limited number of its neighbors, whereas the GAU captures the system-wide interactions. Dynamic gates then weight and combine these local and global representations. We evaluate GraphGHHA on a networked heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) cyber-physical system under representative attack scenarios. Based on our results, the inference latency of GraphGHHA is 89.3\% smaller than that of the standard graph attention layers (for an interaction graph size of 1536), while achieving an accuracy of 0.982 in detecting attacks. These results demonstrate that the proposed attention mechanism can significantly reduce the attack detection latency without compromising accuracy.

title: Synchronizing Automata: Open Problems
comments: This is a revision of a paper with the same title, published in EPTCS 451, 2026, pp. 33--47, arXiv:2608.24245v1. Fixed Proposition 7 and its proof; fixed the word in Conjecture 8 and the definition of the automaton's transitions; a few typos corrected
summary: We survey selected open problems in the theory of synchronizing automata, centered around the famous Černý conjecture. A deterministic finite automaton is called synchronizing if it admits a reset word whose action maps all states to a single state. The Černý conjecture states that every synchronizing automaton with $n$ states possesses a reset word of length at most $(n-1)^2$. We discuss avoiding words, compressing a state with another, synchronization of a (given or any) subset, complexity of deciding the synchronizability, average reset threshold, and linear-algebraic methods. Some new auxiliary results are also presented.
comment: This is a revision of a paper with the same title, published in EPTCS 451, 2026, pp. 33--47, arXiv:2608.24245v1. Fixed Proposition 7 and its proof; fixed the word in Conjecture 8 and the definition of the automaton's transitions; a few typos corrected

title: Resource Allocation for Secure Dual-UAV-Assisted ISAC System
comments: 13 pages,6 figures, accepted by Digital Communications and Networks
summary: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is a rising technology in the next wireless communication networks, enabling the simultaneous execution of communication and sensing tasks by fully utilizing limited spectrum resources. In this work, we investigate the secrecy performance of a dual-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-assisted secure ISAC system. Specifically, a base station UAV communicates with users and transmits radar signals to locate potential eavesdroppers, while simultaneously providing information to a jammer UAV to perform jamming tasks. Considering constraints such as maximum UAV velocity, transmit power, propulsion energy, and sensing thresholds, we maximize the average secrecy rate by optimizing user scheduling strategies, time allocation, transmit power, and UAV trajectories. The presence of a non-convex problem, originating from tightly coupled variables, is tackled by an efficient iterative algorithm. In particular, the original optimization problem is decomposed into six subproblems, and non-convex subproblems are transformed into approximately convex forms via successive convex approximation. Then, block coordinate descent techniques are employed to solve all subproblems sequentially. Numerical results demonstrate the convergence and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
comment: 13 pages,6 figures, accepted by Digital Communications and Networks

title: Meta$^n$: Recursive Self-Improvement through Emergent Depth
summary: Self-improving LLM agents refine answers, not the process that produces those answers. Systems that add a meta-level hold that level fixed, and those that edit themselves must leave part of their own editing machinery untouched to stay stable, capping the meta-depth they realize at roughly two. We present Meta$^n$, which keeps the meta-operation fixed and recurses on its input instead. That operation, $Ω$, is applied repeatedly to its own products, reading the traces of the solver stack below together with the code that produced them, then writing the next layer as a strategic pre-process and a library of callable helpers. Because $Ω$ never changes, it cannot destabilize the system, and because its input strictly grows, each layer reasons from a higher vantage than the last. Depth is set by convergence rather than fixed in advance, and an evolutionary archive searches over layer chains. Across two backbones, Meta$^n$ outperforms prior self-improving agents on all eight benchmark families. The sharpest case is ARC-AGI-2, built to resist skill memorization, where it alone scores above zero. Ablations indicate that most of the gain from recursion comes from the conditioning each layer passes to the next, and distinct layer roles emerge with depth although no prompt prescribes them. Code available at https://github.com/minnesotanlp/meta-n

title: Language Model Security Modules: Turning LLM Interpretability into Runtime Defense
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are served behind layered defenses such as alignment and guardrail models, yet jailbreaks still get through. Interpretability research looks inside the model, where methods such as probes and sparse autoencoders expose signals of harmful content during generation. A signal alone, however, is not a defense. To become one, the serving system must tie each signal to the right request, apply the policy as declared, and release output only when the policy allows. Today, defenses built on such signals handle these duties on their own, so every new detector needs its own integration. Yet none of these duties depends on how a signal is computed. We present Language Model Security Modules (LMSM), which adapts the design of Linux Security Modules to LLM serving and carries out these duties once in a shared mediation path. The path hosts pluggable backends that turn model internals into evidence and policies that decide what that evidence allows. Each policy declares the evidence and evaluations it needs, and LMSM provides exactly these for each request and verifies that they took place, so a failure is never mistaken for permission. Protection therefore remains cheap and correct under common serving optimizations. We evaluate LMSM in vLLM, with both eager and compiled execution, on Qwen3-4B and Gemma-3-4B with fitted probes, a released transcoder, and a released sparse autoencoder. With vLLM's default optimizations on, every backend keeps at least 96% of native throughput, and all of them share the same mediation path. On Qwen3-4B, a representative probe-based policy cuts HarmBench attack success from 39.4% to 3.3% while XSTest false refusals rise from 0.8% to 3.1%. LMSM lets existing and future interpretability methods become runtime defenses without rebuilding the serving path.

title: MetaSieve: Faster Relational Deep Learning through SQL-Based Metapath Selection
comments: Extended version of: Fahim Shahriar Khan and Ashraf Aboulnaga. "MetaSieve: Faster Relational Deep Learning through SQL-Based Metapath Selection," Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment (PVLDB), volume 20, number 3, pp. 636-648, November 2026
summary: Relational Deep Learning (RDL) is an effective approach to machine learning over multi-table relational databases. In RDL, a database is modeled as a graph in which each row is a node and each foreign-key relation is an edge, and a graph neural network (GNN) is trained on this graph. Training a GNN requires sampling a subgraph around every seed node in the training set, and the cost of training is largely determined by the size of these subgraphs. This paper aims to reduce subgraph size by leveraging the join and aggregation capabilities of relational database systems. We observe that sampled subgraphs are obtained by following metapaths composed of foreign-key links, and that many of these metapaths can be pruned without loss of accuracy. We present MetaSieve, a metapath selection layer that determines which metapaths to retain and which to prune. For each candidate metapath extension, MetaSieve computes statistics via SQL join and aggregation queries and evaluates the extension based on a novel scoring function that prefers lightweight but informative candidates. Metapaths whose scores fall below a threshold are deemed uninformative and pruned. Metapath selection in MetaSieve is lightweight since it relies only on database statistics and task labels, and it is independent of GNN parameters, so it integrates with diverse GNN architectures for classification and regression. Our evaluation on the RelBench benchmark with multiple GNN backbones shows that MetaSieve consistently reduces per-epoch training time by large margins while maintaining and often improving accuracy.

title: VOS: Variate Ordering Strategies for Skyline Query Optimization
comments: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data
summary: Efficiency of skyline algorithms is highly influenced by the underlying data characteristics. Traditionally, optimization efforts have focused on minimizing the total number of tuple-pair dominance checks to improve query performance. However, in practice, a dominance check between two tuples does not necessarily require evaluating dominance relationships for each and every preference attribute of the data and this creates a disconnect between dominance checks optimization and query execution performance. In this paper, we argue that skyline algorithms need to optimize total per-attribute dominance checks, along with per-tuple dominance checks and that, for both of these goals, the ordering of the attributes (or variates) can have a substantial impact on the efficiency of skyline computation. Based on this premise, we present several strategies for identifying an effective variate order to minimize redundant attribute comparisons. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, and on both scalar and SIMD architectures, confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach in reducing computational overhead and improving skyline query performance.
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Conference on Big Data

title: MVC-Bench: Benchmarking Calibration of Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Reliable evaluation of vision-language models (VLMs) and medical vision-language models (Medical-VLMs) requires calibrated confidence, particularly under realistic clinical conditions. However, existing efforts mainly focused on improving accuracy, leaving calibration in the medical domain underexplored. To this end, we propose MVC-Bench, a calibration-centric benchmark for medical image classification with VLMs and Medical-VLMs. MVC-Bench assesses the calibration across three axes: (i) robustness to modality, backbone, and domain shift (ii) effectiveness of calibration strategies and prompt-tuning methods (iii) stability under prompt-template and random-seed variations. The benchmark covers eight different backbones, three medical modalities, including fundus imaging, histopathology, and chest X-ray under in-domain and domain shift settings. It compares post-hoc calibration, train-time calibration, and zero-shot inference methods, together with six prompt-tuning methods. Across more than 1638 controlled experiments, we report accuracy and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) as primary metrics, and further report results with complementary calibration measures, including Maximum Calibration Error (MCE) and Adaptive Calibration Error (ACE). We further investigate the underlying causes of miscalibration in VLMs and Medical-VLMs and propose a simple train-time calibration method, Multi-Class Margin (MCM) regularization, which achieves lowest ECE on 10 out of 12 settings in in-domain and remains competitive under domain shifts. Collectively, MVC-Bench provides a structured evaluation framework and actionable guidance for improving calibration in safety-critical medical workflows.

title: Video-OPSD: Exploiting Privileged Visual Evidence for On-Policy Self-Distillation in Video Large Language Models
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has recently emerged as an effective post-training paradigm that provides dense token-level supervision from a privileged self-teacher, yet it remains underexplored for Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs). Existing methods typically construct privileged teachers by augmenting their context with additional information while keeping the primary input unchanged for both teacher and student. In video reasoning, however, privileged information can also be found within the primary input itself: videos contain substantial temporal redundancy, and only a few frames carry the evidence needed to answer a question. Building on this observation, we present $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$, an OPSD framework that exploits privileged visual evidence for both self-teacher construction and knowledge transfer. First, our Evidence-Grounded Self-Teacher conditions the teacher exclusively on annotated evidence frames, while the student reasons over a broader set of frames that contains them. This focused visual context enables more targeted supervision without introducing visual content unavailable to the student. Second, our Evidence-Guided Token Optimization adaptively weights token-level distillation according to an estimate of each reasoning token's reliance on privileged visual evidence, thereby emphasizing perceptually grounded reasoning. Across five video benchmarks and three Qwen-VL backbones, $\textbf{Video-OPSD}$ consistently outperforms Standard OPSD by 1.8-2.3 percentage points on average, establishing an effective and efficient post-training approach for Video-LLMs.

title: How do features act in an individual prediction? Separating standalone and interaction effects with a case-based taxonomy
summary: Local explanation methods such as SHAP and LIME summarize each feature with a single attribution score, and interaction indices quantify how strongly features interact. Neither tells a user how a feature acts in a given prediction: whether its effect is the same alone and in context, or whether the other features amplify it, make it unnecessary, switch it off or reverse it. We extend case-based feature importance (CBFI), originally a global method, to individual predictions. Evaluating the model in four hybrid states per background sample decomposes the in-context importance of a feature into a standalone and an interaction effect, and a case taxonomy labels each feature of an instance as inactive, standalone, amplified, redundant, gated or reversed. We compare the method with k-SII, TreeSHAP interaction values and the H-statistic on synthetic functions, and study eight real tabular datasets with six model families. On the true functions, the decomposition recovered interactions exactly (correlation 0.99 with the analytic local interaction). On fitted models, pair recovery was slightly below that of dedicated indices (local precision@k 0.86-0.91 versus 0.91-0.95). Interaction values alone could not distinguish substitution from gating, whereas the taxonomy identified both without knowing the partner (accuracy 0.74-0.76); applied to Shapley interaction values, it performed comparably. On real data, 45-57% of feature pairs with nearly identical SHAP values received different labels, and in a medical-insurance model the method showed that the interaction component of smoking changes sign at a body-mass index of 30. Localized CBFI does not detect interactions more accurately than existing indices; what it adds is a decomposition into standalone and interaction effects and a label stating how each feature acts.

title: Visual Token Coding for Video Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: In this paper, we propose a new token compression paradigm for video Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), termed Visual Token Coding ($VTC$). Inspired by classical video coding principles, e.g., HEVC, VTC performs structured compression by predicting the I/P frames of a video and measuring their frame-wise residuals to estimate token redundancy. Based on this base paradigm, we further extend VTC with a set of dynamic budgeting designs towards more cost-effective token coding, termed $VTC_{dy}$. To validate VTC and $VTC_{dy}$, we apply them to three MLLMs and conduct experiments on a set of video understanding benchmarks. The experimental results show that as a base paradigm, VTC can achieve an average performance retention of 98.4% on Qwen3-VL under a 50% token compression ratio, and the enhanced $VTC_{dy}$ can further improve the retention to 100.3%, outperforming a set of compared methods. Moreover, as a plug-and-play design, VTC requires no additional tuning of MLLMs for token coding. Our code is given in the supplementary materials.

title: MAP: A Benchmark on Multimodal Accessibility Planning for Real World Places
summary: We introduce MAP, the first benchmark to evaluate multimodal AI systems as assistants for users with accessibility requirements when planning visits to places in the real world. In our evaluation, systems are presented with requests to verify or recommend a point of interest meeting an accessibility requirement. MAP contains two novel assessments: Claim verification for accessibility planning assesses if information on places and stated accessibility features is supported and identifies places that satisfy requested accessibility features. Visual evidence retrieval for accessibility planning checks if a multimodal AI system can select visual evidence for the requested place and accessibility feature. Our methodology supports comparison of AI systems in a setting where place information and accessibility information can change over time by evaluating systems and refreshing ground truth data at scheduled times. The benchmark is based on automatic rating and human rating for a proportion of responses.

title: Predicting Student Attrition in Competitive Programming: A Large-Scale Study Integrating Survey Insights and Global Behavioral Logs
comments: Accepted at International Conference on Emerging Frontiers in Advanced Sciences and Technologies (EFAST 2026). 10 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables
summary: We compared the recorded behavior of competitive programmers who became inactive on Codeforces with that of active users of similar skill. From 6,927 accounts collected via the public Codeforces API in June 2026, we excluded 888 accounts with incomplete submission histories and restricted both cohorts to a peak rating below 1500. This yielded 3,421 active accounts and 908 accounts with no submissions for at least three months, labeled as attrition. Behavioral differences between the two groups were small. Attrition accounts accepted smaller shares of their attempts overall and on mathematics and data-structure problems (rank-biserial r from -0.16 to -0.12), and solved fewer problems per rated contest (median 5.95 vs. 7.80; r = -0.13). Struggle time, upsolving, and recovery after rating drops did not differ significantly after correcting for multiple testing. Two pre-specified models trained on eight observation-window-independent features achieved cross-validated AUROCs of 0.596 (logistic regression) and 0.611 (random forest), yielding predicted probabilities barely above the base rate. Across random samples, stricter filtering rules, alternative definitions of inactivity, and tenure-matched cohorts, AUROC ranged from 0.58 to 0.66. Restricting features to activity from the 6- or 12-month windows ending three months prior to each user's final submission produced AUROCs of 0.59 to 0.65, indicating that minor behavioral differences precede inactivity but remain too weak to reliably identify individual at-risk users. All data and code are publicly archived, with a single command reproducing every reported result.

title: Fair Division Under Boolean Valuations: Beyond Normalization
summary: We study fair division of indivisible items when agents have arbitrary two-level preferences: the value of each agent for any set of items is Boolean, which need not be monotone or additive. Notably, we do not impose the standard assumption of normalization, i.e., different agents may value the empty set at different Boolean levels. Since the preferences are nonmonotone, envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) each admit several variants, depending on which items are tested for removal and whether they are removed from the envious agent's bundle or the envied agent's bundle. This paper investigates the existence of these variants of EF1 and EFX, on their own and together with economic efficiency, incentive compatibility, feasibility constraints, and lottery-based randomization. Our paper presents a wide range of positive and negative results that collectively highlight an interesting phenomenon: the landscape of achievable guarantees depends crucially on the number of normalized agents, who value the empty bundle at the lower Boolean level.

title: Ceiling-Clipped Acceptance Histograms Indicate Stranded Speed-up in Block-Diffusion Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding speeds up generation using an efficient draft model (drafter) to propose tokens that a target model verifies in one pass, preserving the target's output distribution. High-acceptance block-diffusion drafters, such as DFlash and DFlare, fill an entire block in one parallel pass. In many cycles, the target model accepts all draft tokens in the block, so the drafter exhausts its trained horizon before verification ever fails. We call this unrealized acceptance stranded speed-up. Evaluating a drafter by its per-prompt or per-cycle mean committed length alone hides this phenomenon, whereas the acceptance histogram exposes this bottleneck as a spike in the ceiling bin, the fraction of cycles that accept the entire block. We recommend reviewing the acceptance histogram before spending more training compute. Naively widening the block at inference could reduce acceptance for drafters with bidirectional attention, since, once the block outgrows its training size, the drafter's bidirectional attention shifts its distribution even at early positions, which empirically degrades acceptance there. We therefore post-train the drafter to a longer block with a short curriculum that emphasizes the newly exposed positions, a method we call DBloom. We continue training the pretrained DFlash and DFlare drafters at the original block size of 16, before expanding them to 24 (B16 to B24) on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B. Compared to the original B16 drafters, this technique raises per-prompt committed length by up to +1.7 tokens and decode speed-up by a median of +10.2% versus +5.7% without the continuation. On high-ceiling benchmarks, the speed-up rises to +11.9%. On Gemma-4-12B-IT and GPT-OSS-20B, expansion also raises committed length on every benchmark. Against JetSpec, a tree drafter, DBloom has higher committed length by point estimate on every benchmark at tree budgets up to 64 nodes.

title: RadMatch: Auditable Radiology Report Evaluation via Finding-Level Matching
summary: As AI systems are increasingly used to draft radiology reports, reliably evaluating their clinical quality remains a critical challenge. We introduce RadMatch, a multi-stage LLM-based framework that turns report evaluation into a structured, auditable finding-level record. It extracts findings from a reference and a candidate report, matches them by clinical equivalence, grades each match over ten clinical attributes, and gives every match and unmatched finding a verdict and a clinical-significance tier. To validate metrics on CT, we build and release MetricEval-BodyCT, the first public metric-evaluation benchmark of chest and abdomen CT reports annotated by radiologists error by error. On it and three chest X-ray benchmarks, RadMatch with an open 31B judge on consumer GPUs agrees with radiologists more closely than previous published metrics, and even reaches inter-expert agreement on ReXVal and on the significant errors of MetricEval-BodyCT. Radiologists auditing its decisions on 60 studies confirm 98.5% of its matches and 93.6% of the errors it counts. When used to evaluate state-of-the-art radiology report generation models, RadMatch shows that most CT models, unlike several chest X-ray models, actually leave more significant errors than an image-blind normal template, as their added unsupported findings outnumber the reference findings they correctly report. We provide RadMatch's code, its dashboard, the MetricEval-BodyCT dataset and all per-report scores.

title: XMerge: Cross-Axis Selection and Reconstructive Layer Merging for LLM Depth Compression
comments: Accepted as an oral presentation at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop LIGHT: Lightweight Trustworthy Foundation Models. 21 pages, 5 figures, 25 tables. v2: camera-ready version
summary: Removing complete transformer layers preserves a standard serving architecture, but existing depth-compression methods can lose substantial quality, and the loss varies unpredictably across models. We introduce XMerge, a post-training method with two components. Cross-axis selection identifies a block with low relative-magnitude and angular hidden-state change, and local boundary reconstruction re-fits the adjacent surviving block to match the original two-block output. XMerge uses no task labels or end-to-end fine-tuning, and it introduces neither architectural changes nor additional inference-time parameters. Across seven Llama and Qwen backbones (0.5B-8B), five published baselines, and three layer-reduction levels, its advantage over baselines is largest at the most aggressive removal: at k=4 it ranks first on six of seven backbones on CORE (a 22-task aggregate) and, separately, on six of seven on MMLU (five of seven on both at once), while avoiding the large perplexity increases of several competing operators. In a task-level bootstrap, the 95% confidence intervals for the three largest CORE margins exclude zero; the remaining margins are consistent with ties. Across the 14 (model, regime) cells it is also the only evaluated operator that never collapses, ranking top-2 in both zero-shot and in-context regimes; on a first calibration probe (one backbone) it is the best-calibrated operator. Ablations show that local reconstruction provides most of the gain, while cross-axis fusion helps when the two selection axes disagree. The additional construction cost is recovered through per-token decode savings after roughly tens of thousands of requests.

title: Adapting a Foundation Model for Lunar Surface Height Estimation
summary: Digital elevation models (DEMs) can provide accurate height information, making it invaluable for analyzing the lunar surface. Due to recent advancements in computer vision, the focus is on generating DEMs using monocular depth estimation via deep learning. Classic lunar crater detection methods rely mainly on 2D image data. Our goal is to address this issue by developing a relative lunar surface height estimator that could provide additional information for crater localization. In this letter, we present a methodology that builds on the zero-shot relative depth estimation model Depth Anything V2 (DAV2). Other works have been using it as a state-of-the-art comparison for their proposed lunar DEM estimation method, but without adaptations to the target domain. Thus, it may underperform. Therefore, we propose a fine-tuning strategy with publicly available SPG-derived DEM data of the lunar surface, and refer to it as DEM-DAV2. Specifically, we introduce new learnable parameters in the Transformer-based encoder with low-rank adaptation (LoRA), and we unfreeze certain layers in the model's decoder. On our test set, the proposed DEM-DAV2 reduces the average MAE and RMSE by $\sim$80\% and $\sim$79\%, respectively, compared to the zero-shot DAV2. This demonstrates a significant improvement in performance compared to the zero-shot model, effectively transforming DAV2 into a reliable relative height estimator of the lunar surface. However, the predictions remain relative and require scale recovery from a low-resolution DEM such as SLDEM.

title: Two Principles for Autoregressive Language Modeling
summary: We investigate the functional differentiation learned by RoPE Transformers to derive principles for autoregressive language modeling. We introduce two intervention-based metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS) measures how removing a frequency contribution changes a head's full attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD) isolates the effect of rotary modulation. In Qwen3 and Llama3.1, these metrics distinguish retrieval from positional modeling, while individual heads can exhibit both functions. A mid-low-frequency Global Positional Band (GPBand) separates their frequency dependencies and tracks the training sequence length in controlled experiments, suggesting that global positional fitting can hinder zero-shot length extrapolation. These findings motivate two principles. (1) Functional Organization: retrieval and positional functions should be assigned separately and mixed within layers with layer-specific allocation; and (2) Positional Dependence: positional modeling should operate only locally, while global access should rely on position-independent retrieval. Matched pretraining from scratch and targeted architectural ablations at 380M and 1.4B parameters support both principles and highlight the importance of mechanism choice in realizing each function. Together, these findings suggest a promising route toward architectural innovation grounded in the functional requirements of autoregressive language modeling.

title: OracleZoom: Reference-Constrained Recursive Image Super-Resolution Beyond Ground Truth
summary: Recursive image Super-Resolution (SR) reaches extreme magnification by feeding each prediction back into the same model, like zooming into an image again and again. Real ground truth for deep zooms is impractical to capture (a full $256\times$ target would be a 52 GB image), so predictions at deeper zooms have no supervision. Yet the last ground-truth image still contains the region that every deeper zoom magnifies. OracleZoom turns this region into a training signal. Inspired by on-policy self-distillation, the model trains on its own prediction for one recursive step ($4\times \rightarrow 16\times$), and a cross-scale loss projects each $16\times$ prediction back to the last ground truth at $4\times$. This projection can verify only coarse content, so a no-reference quality objective guides the remaining fine detail, and a latent prior stops this objective from adding hallucinated artifacts. On seven datasets, OracleZoom achieves the highest CLIPIQA at every zoom depth (mean 0.713 vs. 0.621 for Chain-of-Zoom), with the largest gains at the deepest zooms, even though training stops at $16\times$ and optimizes a different quality metric. Pooled over two ground-truth-anchored judges, this added detail comes at the same hallucination rate as Chain-of-Zoom at $16\times$ and a lower rate at $4\times$, and removing the cross-scale loss raises hallucination at $16\times$.

title: TabBench-Bio: A Living Benchmark for Machine Learning on High-Dimensional Biomedical Tables
summary:
Biomedical tables often combine thousands of measured variables with only tens or hundreds of labelled samples, a regime that is poorly represented in general-purpose tabular benchmarks. We introduce TabBench-Bio, a living and interactive benchmark of 43 biomedical datasets spanning multiple domains. Under a shared cross-validation protocol, we compare classical estimators, neural networks, and tabular foundation models across 28 feature-by-sample operating points. At the reference cell of 10,000 features and 100 training samples, RealTabPFN 2.5 has the highest point estimate, closely followed by TabPFN 3 and Logistic Regression. A paired bootstrap over the target pool separates RealTabPFN 2.5 from TabPFN 3 by 87 Elo (95\% interval [43, 129]).
  Tabular foundation models generally occupy the leading ranks, while the strongest configuration depends on the operating point and biomedical modality. The AutoML framework AutoGluon, using its one-hour "extreme" preset, is configured as a separate resource-intensive reference and reported here at the reference and full cell. Fold-level predictions, run status, and deterministic aggregations make every reported result reproducible and reusable. The benchmark is open to contributions of new biomedical datasets.
  The interactive leaderboard is available at https://tabbench-bio.eu.

title: Improving Cross-Lingual Token Representations by Adding a Pinch of SALT
summary: Cross-lingual sentence encoders enable scalable transfer across hundreds of languages, powering applications such as translation mining and zero-shot learning in low-resource settings. Although trained for sentence-level alignment, they are increasingly also applied to token-level tasks such as hallucination detection and sequence tagging, exposing a mismatch between training and usage. We propose SALT, a lightweight post-training method that improves token representations by injecting span-level supervision into existing sentence encoders. Across five multilingual token-level benchmarks, SALT achieves the best overall results on four of them, outperforming alternative fine-tuning strategies and competitive encoders. It also improves sentence-level performance on cross-lingual retrieval and classification tasks. These results demonstrate that span-level supervision is an effective signal for improving both token and sentence representations.

title: Threshold Choice, Not Sample Size, Bounds Trustless Verification of Nondeterministic Compound AI Workflows
summary: Compound AI pipelines chain LLM calls, retrievers, and tools and are nondeterministic: sampling, model updates, and volatile tool responses make one input yield different outputs across runs. Such pipelines increasingly run across edge, cloud, and orbital nodes owned by no single party, whose optimizations discard intermediate results before inspection. Verifying reproduction there means tolerating nondeterministic outputs, a node that may not report honestly, and intermittent access to any shared record; existing work addresses at most two at once. We give a protocol covering all three: it commits digests of each stage's inputs, outputs, and context under a policy digest pinning the metric and threshold, anchors them without trusting the executing node, defers under partition, and decides a challenge on the median of $k$ re-executions, with no quorum. Where that procedure breaks is the main result. On a synthetic HotpotQA pipeline a calibrated fixed threshold accepts 44 of 45 honest reproductions and rejects 104 of 105 divergent pairs, yet lets same-input fabrication through in 27 of 29 trials at k=5, more samples being no help since sampling sharpens an estimate without moving it. Holding that metric and this pipeline's re-execution spread fixed, the binding constraint is the threshold rather than the sample size: one derived per execution detects 19 of 29 where the best constant matched to the same zero honest rejections reaches 9, rejects no honest commitment at k=5 though 3 of 15 at k=3, and catches 11 of 15 of an attacker built against it, which has to aim at a target drawn only after its commitment exists. That rule is measured rather than deployed.

title: Morphology-Aware Human Motion Retargeting for Wheeled-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comments: 8 pages, 11 figures, 9 tables. Version 2 extends the motion-retargeting method to account for wheeled-base stability and adds corresponding ablation studies
summary: We propose a whole-body teleoperation method for topology-mismatched humanoids, with a focus on motion retargeting and whole-body control for wheeled humanoids. First, we design a Topology-Adaptive Motion Retargeting (TAMR) method with a robust switching logic that selects mapping joints according to human posture. Second, we train a Teacher-Student DAgger method that supports real-time teleoperation with inertial motion capture and virtual-reality devices. We further develop a Temporal Feasibility-Aware Command Governor (T-FeaCG) for the wheeled base to reduce the mismatch between teleoperation policy intent and the feasible execution margin of a three-steer-wheel base. We will release the complete teleoperation code and dataset, and demonstrate whole-body humanoid skills learned from teleoperation. More videos are available at: https://xiachenbuo.github.io/Morphology-Aware-Human-Motion-Retargeting-for-Wheeled-Humanoid-Loco-Manipulation/.
